projects.name: Ghostframe
projects.blurb: Pose see-through ghosts of Tesla Optimus around a stage and watch it walk and jump through every in-between frame.
body: Ghostframe is a pose-to-pose animation toy starring Tesla Optimus. Every keyframe is a ghost, a see-through copy of the robot that you place on the stage and pose by grabbing a hand, a foot, the head or the hips and pulling. The part you are moving lights up blue, and the ghost you are editing turns into the real, shaded robot so you can judge the pose in depth.

Everything between the ghosts is generated. Poses blend along smooth curves through time, but when two ghosts stand apart Optimus does not slide across the floor: the app plans real footsteps, plants each foot and rolls it from heel to toe, sways the hips and swings the arms against the legs, with the slightly bent knees of a robot gait. Switch a transition to Jump and you get a crouch, a flight with tucked legs and a landing that soaks up the impact. The robot itself is built entirely in code from lofted shells on a 49-bone rig, with no model files.

Try this first: press play on the demo, then click a ghost, pull its hand above its head, drag the ring under its feet somewhere new and play it again. Turn on Klatki (frames) to see every generated frame laid out as a trail of faint robots.

projects.name: Rug Rush
projects.blurb: Unload rug trucks, read the care labels and wash every rug in a co-op warehouse without ruining the silk.
body: A first-person co-op game for 1 to 4 players about running a rug cleaning warehouse. Trucks back up with rolled rugs: drag them out, kick them open, read the ISO care label on a corner and pick from 26 cleaning products, powders, gels, sprays and foam that layer on top of each other. Then scrub, rinse under the hanging hose, squeegee the water into the drain, dry it, wrap it on the roller and load it onto the outbound truck.

Every rug is real cloth made of its own fibre: wool, silk, sisal, cotton, polyester or polypropylene. They react differently, so the wrong product runs the colours, fades the silk or felts the wool, and that damage stays. Dirt, water, soap and damage live in per-rug textures, the water on the floor is a GPU shallow water simulation that flows along the grout, and online co-op runs over WebRTC with a public room list.

Try this first: aim at a stain with empty hands to see what it is and how to treat it on that particular rug, or press T to ask Rug Buddy, an AI assistant that can see your whole warehouse. Then foam up a rug and rinse it with the hose.

projects.name: Fabrics
projects.blurb: Pull curtains, fly flags, drape robes and scrunch rugs, then cut, burn, dye and blow on real-time cloth.
body: A textile playground in the browser. Six scenes, each built around one piece of fabric: sheer curtains on a rod with sliding rings, a flag in the wind, a velvet robe on a dress form, a Persian rug, a tablecloth over a laid table and a hammock. Swap the fabric at any time between silk, chiffon, linen, velvet, denim and wool, pick one of nine prints and any colour.

The cloth is simulated thread by thread with a small physics engine written for it, and every fabric behaves differently: chiffon floats and tears first, denim is stiff, velvet is heavy, silk slides. Pull too hard and it rips along the threads. Fire spreads faster upwards and chars the edges, while wool chars and puts itself out. Dye bleeds into the weave and mixes like real dye, so blue over yellow turns green. The sounds are real recordings.

Try this first: pull the curtains open, then switch to the tablecloth and yank it off the table fast, like a magician. Throw balls of yarn into the hammock, set the robe alight, and turn on the thread view in the studio settings to see stretched threads glow. On a phone you can tilt it to pour gravity or blow into the microphone for wind.

projects.name: Roadster Jump
projects.blurb: Suction the Roadster up a giant curled ramp, hang from the ceiling, then kickflip off the lip on cold-gas jets.
body: A stunt game built on the arena from Jurek's film Roadster Kickflip. You walk up to the Tesla Roadster as Jurek, get in through the gullwing door and drive at a 25 metre ramp that curls over into an upside-down ceiling. Turn on the suction fan and the car sticks to the wall, then to the ceiling, where it can hang upside down for as long as you like.

Everything is physics. The car comes from Roadster 88: raycast suspension that follows the car's own down axis, real tyre grip and ten gimballed cold-gas nozzles run by a small flight computer. The fan pushes the car onto whatever surface it faces, harder the more it hangs upside down, so the curl works at any speed. Leave the lip upside down and the arrow keys roll and flip the car on thrust. Flight assist can level the wheels before touchdown and turn the jets into a soft landing.

Try this first: press F for suction, drive up and stop on the ceiling, reverse down, then run at it with half throttle and roll with the arrows after the lip. A film-style 540 kickflip lands right on the painted X. Every landed jump is scored, P replays it from TV cameras in slow motion, and the best jump, the longest jump and the most rotation go on online leaderboards. Works on phones with touch controls.

projects.name: Spillway
projects.blurb: Draw gutters with a limited marker and pump your colour of water into its cup, alone or with up to three friends online.
body: A co-op water puzzle for 1 to 4 players. Every player owns one colour of water and a plunger at the top of a long side-scrolling map. Draw gutters with a marker that runs out of ink, hold the plunger and steer your water past rocks, wind and no-draw zones into the cup of your colour. Anything that misses falls into the abyss.

The water is a particle fluid written for the game and it is fully deterministic, so online play only sends inputs: the host keeps the clock, everyone else simulates the same world a fraction of a second behind and checks it against the host. If the host leaves, another player takes over without losing a drop. Each colour is rendered in its own channel, so streams that touch stay crisp.

Try this first: draw a line from under your tank down to your cup, then hold Space. Later, route every colour into the mixer, which turns them into rainbow water that pays double. Money is shared, the shop between levels is a little scrolling street with funnels, pipes, trampolines, fans, lifts, ice and magnets, and the Continue button at the end takes the whole room to the next level.

projects.name: Mirage
projects.blurb: Put on smart glasses, call drones down from orbit and project a dragon, a whale or outer space over Venice.
body: A sandbox in a Venetian district built entirely in code: canals and bridges, a church with a campanile and over six hundred houses with real window openings and furnished rooms behind the glass. You play Jurek's own avatar wearing Gzowo Glass, while the sassy assistant G.L.A.S.S. comments on everything from the HUD.

The glasses link to the GZOWO LABS satellite, which drops a swarm of drones. Every illusion is split into cells and each cell needs one drone, so you choose how many to send: too few and the dragon, the T-rex or the space dome gets ragged glowing holes with the drones visible inside. Projections build up as holograms, then turn photoreal, and when they attack, the drones hidden inside fire for real: glass shatters, balconies fall, tourists run.

Try this first: press G to call drones, hold Q and pick the dragon, set the drone count with the mouse wheel and click. Then aim at it, press F and choose Attack. You can also climb any house with Space, row a gondola with E or ride a drone with B.

projects.name: Timeblock
projects.blurb: Drop in a video and it turns into a block of time cast in sanded resin, where every frame is a slice.
body: Timeblock stacks the frames of a video one behind another, so time becomes the depth of a block of frosted resin. Anything that stands still melts away and only the motion is left: a spinning propeller turns into a spiral, a bouncing ball into a row of arches, a ripple into a cone.

The block is a real volume, not a picture glued to a cube. The frames sit in a 3D texture and every pixel shoots a ray through it, blurring more the deeper it goes, the way sanded resin does. The still background is found with a per-pixel median over time, shaky hand-held clips are lined up first, and the sanding scratches catch the light as you turn the block. A photo gets a relief instead, with the subject lifted off its backdrop.

Try this first: drop in a short clip filmed with a steady hand, turn the block with your mouse or finger, then drag Skos (slant) to cut it at an angle and see the past and the future in one picture. When you like it, save a PNG or a 6 second MP4.

projects.name: Speak & Groove
projects.blurb: Type a letter and a robot voice spells it through a big reverb, then a techno band joins in behind you.
body: A talking toy groovebox in the spirit of the 1978 spelling toy. Every key you press is spoken by a crunchy 8 kHz robot voice drenched in reverb. Keep typing and the band joins in, one layer every two bars: pad, 909 kick and hats, an acid bassline, clap, arpeggiator, swung percussion, vocal chops and a funky clav. Stop typing and it peels back down to the pad and the echo.

Everything follows what you type. A to G are literally their notes in A minor, the last letter picks the next chord, and the last sixteen letters become the bassline and the arpeggio. The voice is real LPC speech synthesis, the same trick the original chip used, running in an AudioWorklet so it can sing in key without turning into a chipmunk.

Try this first: put headphones on, type your name, then press Enter and it spells it back on the beat. Drag the stylus around the round stylophone, smear the whole mix on the touch FX pad, and on a laptop pinch the trackpad for more space or scroll for the acid filter.

projects.name: Toot Tube
projects.blurb: Up to three animals hang on to one inflatable ring and steer it down a spiky river the only way they can: by farting.
body: Toot Tube is a co-op river race for one to three players. Everyone is an animal (capybara, frog, pig, penguin or duck) holding on to the outside of the same swim ring, and the only engine is gas. Toot and the ring is pushed away from you, so to go forward somebody first has to swim around to the back.

Online, the ring is split into slices with barriers between them, one slice per player, and nobody can swim into a friend's part. Steering turns into a conversation about who toots, who waits and who ducks. A kilometre of river runs through a spike slalom, spinning sweeper bars you dive under, whirlpools, rapids and a waterfall, gates that open and close, and a final gauntlet. Touch purple spikes or get swept off and the whole crew goes back to the last checkpoint while the clock keeps running.

It runs in the browser with no build step. The river is a path of straights and arcs with its own width, current and drop, the ring has a small 2D physics model, and the host's ring is the shared truth while every player moves their own animal locally, so your toots feel instant. The sounds are real CC0 recordings, twelve of them farts. Try this first: play solo, swim to the back with A or D and hold Space.

projects.name: Cutlery
projects.blurb: Fork, Knife and Butter find their way back to the breakfast table, each one a tool the others need.
body: A wordless 2.5D co-op platformer in the spirit of Unravel Two. Fork, Knife and Butter are not tied together: they help each other by being what they are. Fork stabs into bread, sponges and soft Butter and climbs them, Knife cuts string and sticks into wood as a springy ledge, and Butter hardens in the cold, softens by the stove, melts into an oily puddle that pours through a grate, and floats across a sink with the other two riding on top.

The game opens in a dollhouse cut open from the front, and everyone playing at that moment is in the same house. You pick one character at the door and ride a brass cage lift between the floors. Each floor is one story: Butter's three chapters are for one player, Fork and Knife's for two, the top floor for all three. Stand on a portal with the right characters and the chapter starts for your group, each player on their own device.

Nine chapters cross the whole house: the fridge, the pantry and the living room piano, the cutlery drawer, a dining table with a serving spoon seesaw, a study with a falling ruler, then breakfast, the washing up and the dark kitchen at night. Everything that moves is a kinematic body in a 2D physics world, so online play only sends positions and a few flags. Try this first: enter as Butter, take Cold Start on the ground floor and let the fridge freeze you hard enough to shove a jar.

projects.name: Kindling
projects.blurb: Stick monsters crawl out of a cornfield. Cut them apart with a laser, jump the iron wall and feed the fire.
body: A Halloween defense game in a moonlit cemetery. Monsters made of sticks walk out of the corn toward you, and every cut matters: take a leg and they limp, take both and they crawl, take the arms and they cannot grab you. Thick branches burn through slower than twigs, and every cut end keeps glowing like an ember.

When a round runs out of monsters, an iron barrier rises behind them and plows everything you cut across the field toward you. Jump it at the right moment and the whole pile tips into the fire pit behind you, which grows with every round.

Every stick, whole or cut, is drawn by one instanced mesh with its own shader for bark, bends, cut rings and embers, so a field of monsters and their broken pieces stays cheap. The monsters walk on procedural skeletons that plant their feet, and the pieces you cut off fall as real physics bodies.

Between nights you hang out on Graveyard Hill: spend Candy Corn on new lasers and upgrades, try hats in the wardrobe, practise on the range, race up the gravestone parkour and ring the chapel bell when you are ready. Keys 1 to 4 are emotes. Desktop only, and you can load your own music for the night and the hill in the settings.

projects.name: Campfire
projects.blurb: Sit by a campfire in a dark forest: stack logs, stir the embers, toast a marshmallow or put it all out.
body: A realistic campfire that burns in your browser. Every log keeps track of its own heat, char and fuel, so fire creeps along the wood, jumps to the log next to it, cracks the surface into glowing char and finally collapses into the ember bed. Pull a burning log out of the ring and it slowly dies down to a smoulder.

The flames are a real volume, not flat sprites. Each frame the burning logs are drawn into a small 3D flame field, and a raymarcher eats it away with rising noise until it breaks into licking tongues. That is why the fire follows the wood when you drag a log around. The flickering light casts moving shadows, sparks rise on the plume, and your eyes adapt to the dark when the fire goes out.

Try this first: put headphones on, click the fire to stir it, then press and hold on the embers to blow. Grab a log from the woodpile, toast a marshmallow until it is golden (not black), and finish with a bucket of water to hear the hiss.

projects.name: Cube Breakers
projects.blurb: Shoot balls that bounce forever into a giant cube of blocks, together with everyone who is online.
body: A co-op first-person game on a sunny meadow. In the middle stands a 16 by 16 by 16 cube of glossy blocks, and everybody who opens the page breaks the same one. Your launcher fires balls that fly without gravity at a constant speed and bounce forever off blocks, the ground and each other, chipping damage off every block they touch, until they die on the hexagon force field around the meadow.

The outer shell pops in one hit, the inner layers get much tougher, and the core is built for many sessions. Broken blocks drop loot that floats above the grass. Carry it to the Ball Shop, recycle it for gems and spend them on MultiBalls, BoomBalls, MegaBalls and five other ball types, or on upgrades like Power, Fire Rate, a double jump and a jetpack. When the cube is gone, the next shape grows out of the ground: a pyramid, a sphere, a tower, a GSP rocket and a donut.

There is no game server. Every hit is an atomic increment in a realtime database, every browser decides on its own when a block is gone, and the player who has been online the longest runs the physics of falling chunks for everyone. Try this first: dig a tunnel with a BoomBall, then shoot an AeroBall into it and watch it rattle around inside.

projects.name: Roadster 88
projects.blurb: Drive, boost and fly the 2026 Tesla Roadster on ten cold-gas thrusters, then hit 88 mph and jump through time.
body: A photoreal browser game about the new Tesla Roadster with the SpaceX package. It drives like a 950 kW electric car, fires its rear thrusters for a boost, and lifts off on ten vectored cold-gas nozzles: four at the back, two in the front corners and four under the sills. Jurek's own avatar sits at the wheel.

Flying is real physics, not an animation. A small flight computer splits the force and turn you ask for across all ten nozzles, so hops, hovering and spinning in the air come from differential thrust. The body dents and folds in crashes, and the white vapour plumes are flipbooks rendered in Blender to match the unveil footage.

Try this first: hold Shift on the long straight, then tap Space to hop and hold it to hover. Press T to arm the time circuits, press C for the cockpit, pick a date on the touchscreen and floor it to 88 mph.

projects.name: Wolisz?!
projects.blurb: A 2D online sandbox where every would-you-rather question gives your avatar a power, and the powers pile up.
body: Wolisz?! asks a would-you-rather question at the top of the screen, and whatever you pick really happens to your avatar. Would you rather teleport to wherever you poop, or fly but only one meter above the ground? Pick one, and you get the power. Then the next question stacks a new power on top of the old ones.

Up to ten players join a room with a four-letter code, each picks an avatar colour, and everybody runs around the same 1998-style GeoCities world with all their strange powers at once. There is no winner and no cooldowns, just chaos: poop portals, banana peels, ice trails, bombs, magnets, jetpacks and giant stomping.

The game is plain Canvas 2D with hand-written physics. Every player simulates their own avatar and a realtime database only carries positions and small events like explosions and swaps, so it also runs on a phone in landscape. Start with the poop teleport and see how long it takes your friends to step in it.

projects.name: Make Your Own Game, I'm Lazy
projects.blurb: Draw a tree, a hero and a gun, say what game you want, and an AI writes it around your drawings.
body: Nobody has made anything yet when you start. You and up to five friends type one shared description of the game (everyone's text is underlined in their own colour), then draw every asset: vector or pixel art, with an optional rig so it walks and a recorded sound. Press Done and Haiku asks questions, tells you what is still missing and then writes the game.

Your drawings are not pictures pasted on top. A tree can fall apart into five logs, a cursor becomes that player's own mouse pointer, a bomb explodes when sliced. The game code is written live against a small SDK, tested headless in a sandboxed frame, and repaired automatically if it breaks.
Try the Fruit Ninja idea first, then press Feedback and tell it what is wrong.

projects.name: Foamwalker
projects.blurb: A hunched purple alien with a human face crawls through a foam-block maze.
body: You are a very tall alien made of purple blocks, wearing a very calm human face, lost in a colourful foam playground. Find the glowing cores, then walk into the beam of the UFO overhead to go home.

The walk is fully procedural: four limbs placed with two-bone inverse kinematics, a diagonal trot, and a head that turns to stare at the camera whenever you stop. Foam discs lying around can be kicked across the maze.
Try holding E. The alien dances to a beat that is synthesized live in the browser, and the face breaks into a smile.

projects.name: iPhone Duo
projects.blurb: A semi-realistic virtual clone of the iPhone Duo

projects.name: Wordshader
projects.blurb: Type a line of words and watch a glowing 3D blob and its soundtrack appear letter by letter, then export the loop as a video.
body:
Wordshader is a toy for making short video loops out of words. You type a line,
`yellow spinny torus`, `blobby shiny metallic`, `loop(3) … loopend`, and a glowing
three-dimensional shape rebuilds itself with every keystroke, on a gradient
background, with a soundtrack written the same way. When you like what you see, you
export the loop as a video.

Nothing in it is a model file. The shape is a distance field: a short piece of maths
that, for any point in space, answers how far that point is from the surface. Every
word you type edits that equation, and the picture is drawn by shooting a ray from
each pixel and stepping along it until it hits the surface. That is why the shape can
change on the fly with no loading, no meshes and no waiting, there is nothing to
rebuild, only an equation to re-solve, sixty times a second.

The soundtrack shares the shape's clock. A pulse in the geometry and a beat in the
music are the same number, so the animation lands exactly where the loop restarts and
the exported clip repeats seamlessly instead of stuttering back to the start.

projects.name: Timberline Express
projects.blurb: Survive an endless mountain forest by turning a hand-pumped rail cart into a steam-powered, house-sized train.
body: Timberline Express is a first-person survival game on rails. You start on a hand-pumped rail cart in an endless mountain forest with a few berries in your pocket. You chop trees and crack boulders into stone, forage for mushrooms and hunt deer, then craft your way up from stone tools to a workbench, a furnace, a steam engine and finally an electric locomotive. Every piece of the train is built by hand, right on the moving deck.

The world never ends. Terrain, forests, ponds and a whole branching rail network are generated around you as you travel, with junctions you throw by hand, fallen trees across the tracks and valleys that climb into snowy passes. A day lasts twenty minutes, nights bring wolves, and the weather can turn into a thunderstorm while you are still out collecting wood.

Everything you hold is animated by real two-bone inverse kinematics: your right hand grips high on the pickaxe handle and your left low, a knife spins in your fingers when you draw it, and every swing lands on the exact frame of impact. All sounds are real recordings, and the steam engine is simulated down to its firebox, boiler pressure, safety valve and water tank.
It is a Windows download and runs on a gaming laptop. Co-op for up to four players is being built right now.

projects.name: Haystack Inc.
projects.blurb: Somewhere in a stack of a million straws there is one needle. Dig by hand, then build the machines that dig for you.
body: Haystack Inc. is a first-person game about the most literal search problem there is. Somewhere inside a stack of a million straws sits exactly one needle, and the only way to find it is to take the stack apart. Every straw you see on the stack is a real one: you hold the mouse, it slides out, and it is yours to carry, throw or sell.

A straw sells for a dollar in the machine in the corner, and that dollar buys the first tool. Then a pitchfork that rips out eight at once, a basket, a leaf blower, a hay vacuum, conveyor belts you draw across the yard with a remote, splitters and merges, and finally auto pullers that reach into the stack by themselves while hoppers and sell bins keep the line moving.

The needle is not marked anywhere. It sits at one physical spot under the surface straws, and you only see it once enough hay around it is gone. Sell it and the game is won, then you get to keep running the farm.

Up to four farmers can dig together online: one hosts, the others type a five-letter room code, no accounts needed. Haystack Inc. is a Windows download, not a browser game: it is built in Godot, and the stack alone is 150,000 individual straws.

download.note: Windows 10/11 · unzip and run HaystackInc.exe · online co-op with room codes

projects.name: Hello Miner
projects.blurb: Program mining drones in a tiny Python-like language and automate a floating quarry together with friends in real time.
body: print("Hello, Miner") is a co-op game about not doing the work yourself. You get one floating tile of rock and one drone, and the only way to mine is to write a program: `mine()`, then `move(right)`, then a loop, then a function. Ore pays for a research tree that unlocks a bigger quarry, faster drones, richer ore and new language features, and the fun is watching your code run tile by tile in a bright low-poly world.

The language is deliberately not Python. It looks like it, parentheses, colons, indentation, but the editor indents for you, the parser forgives sloppy whitespace, and every error is a short sentence a nine-year-old can act on. The whole interpreter is custom, which is what lets a drone visibly pause on the exact line it is executing.

Multiplayer is the twist. Everyone in a room shares one mine, one wallet and one research tree, but each player has their own drone and their own code window in their own colour. Any player can type into any window, and you see everyone's cursors live, so an older sibling can fix a bug in a younger one's program without taking over.
Powiązane: [[modular]], [[gzowos-games]], [[stack]], [[agent-workflow]], [[gauntlet-skill]], [[design]].

projects.name: Gzowo Glass
projects.blurb: Home-built smart glasses with a see-through HUD and a voice assistant that talks back in Polish.
body:
Gzowo Glass is a pair of home-built smart glasses with a see-through heads-up
display in front of the right eye and a voice assistant called G.L.A.S.S. (Gzowo
Like A Smart Sass). You press a button on the temple, ask
something in Polish, and the answer comes back both as speech in a tiny speaker by
your ear and as a few lines of text floating over the world.

The optics are the Google Glass trick, not a Hollywood waveguide: a small OLED
screen, a lens that lets your eye focus on something two centimetres away, and a
half-silvered mirror at 45 degrees. Because an OLED's black is truly black, whatever
is black on the screen is simply transparent in front of your eye.

The whole thing runs on a coin-sized ESP32-S3 board with a camera and a microphone.
The glasses draw their own little operating system, boot screen, clock, menus,
timers, and stream your voice and camera frames to a server at home that talks to
a realtime AI model. The frame is 3D-printed to fit one specific face.

projects.name: Squish
projects.blurb: A silent paper-white void full of squishies and fidget toys you can actually squeeze, crack and stretch.
body:
Squish is a silent, paper-white 3D void with a single row of fidget toys and
squishies. There is no interface beyond two faint chevrons at the bottom that fly
the camera to the next toy. Once you are there, you press, grab, stretch and crack
whatever is in front of you with the cursor and hear it respond.

Every toy is a real soft body: a volumetric mesh of particles and springs solved
each frame, so squeezing a gel cube pushes material out to the sides and lets it
slowly recover, while a wax shell breaks along stressed springs into pieces that
fall off. Nothing is a pre-baked animation.

The ASMR is generated live. Instead of looping recordings, the audio engine
listens to the physics and turns deformation speed, stretch and spring breakage
into granular noise, crackles and pops, so no two squeezes sound the same.
Powiązane: [[gzowo-bowling]], [[gzowo-labs]], [[design]], [[game-assets]], [[pytania]].

projects.name: Doodle Run
projects.blurb: A 2D runner where you draw every single thing in it first, then rig your scribbles so they walk, flap and chase you.
body:
DoodleRun is a 2D runner where nothing exists until you draw it. Before anyone
runs, the room splits a list of thirteen slots between the players, ground
tiles, six kinds of creature, coins, three layers of background, and each of you
claims a slot and paints it. Everyone also draws their own character. Then the
game builds an endless track out of your scribbles and you run it together, on
shared fate: if one player dies, everybody restarts.

The interesting part is the rig. A drawing is just a flat picture, so to make a
monster walk you drop a few labelled points on it, left leg, right leg, head,
and the engine treats the drawing as a rubber sheet stretched over a mesh. Each
point pulls the pixels around it, so the legs swing and the body wobbles without
anything ever being cut apart. Your monster stays exactly the drawing you made;
it just starts moving.

Everything runs on plain Canvas 2D with hand-written physics and no build step,
and drawings travel between players as small PNGs, about three kilobytes each,
which is why a whole hand-drawn world fits through a realtime database meant for
positions and scores.

projects.name: Smendilendi Bureau
projects.blurb: Run a tiny architecture practice with your friends, draw the walls, take the client's notes, then walk the finished building thirty years later.

projects.name: Mark Zero
projects.blurb: Fly a powered armor suit at the speed of sound, six degrees of freedom, no rails, no limits.
body:
Mark Zero is a browser flight sandbox built around one question: what would a powered
armor suit actually feel like to fly? You start as a person on foot. You step onto a
platform, the suit assembles itself around you plate by plate, and then the sky is yours
up to the edge of the stratosphere.

The flight model is six degrees of freedom with thrust in body-local axes, which sounds
technical but produces something simple and satisfying: spin around mid-flight while
still travelling forward, hit the throttle, and your own engines slam you to a stop.
That hard brake is not a scripted move, it falls out of the physics. Hands and leg
thrusters animate automatically to match the thrust vector, so it looks like you are
steering with your palms while you are really flying a full 6DOF craft.

The suit is a separate entity from the player, not a costume. Leave it standing in a
field and walk away. Call it and it flies to you across the map and closes around you
mid-stride. Eject at three hundred metres per second and you fall as a person while the
armor chases you down and catches you before the ground does.

projects.name: Noclip
projects.blurb: A found-footage Backrooms experience, you fall in, something tall follows, and the tape keeps rolling.

projects.name: Voidworks
projects.blurb: A factory hanging in white nothing. Droppers, belts, upgraders, and a hard cap on how much can be moving at once.
body: Build a production line suspended in empty white space, no floor, no horizon, and a camera that can fly underneath it. Droppers feed material onto belts, upgraders raise its value, and a green sell plate turns it into money.

The whole game is one constraint: only so many items can exist on the belts at once. A dropper adds one, the sell plate removes one, and when you hit the ceiling the droppers visibly stall. That turns every metre of belt into a real cost and makes the question "what is one slot worth?" the thing you actually play.

There are two families of upgrader and the shapes tell you which is which: tall thin posts multiply, low wide ones add. Adders are flat, so they pay off on cheap material; multipliers scale, so they pay off on expensive material. Adding first and multiplying second measures 2.42x better than the reverse.

projects.name: Ducks
projects.blurb: Feed rubber ducks to a hungry pit, then build the machines that do it for you.
body: A physics co-op sandbox for up to four people. You pick up rubber ducks and throw them into a thirty-two-sided pit that has no bottom, and every duck pays. The money buys machines, walls, tunnels and fans, and the arc of a session is the trip from carrying ducks by hand to watching a factory do it without you.

It looks like a PlayStation game on purpose: flat-shaded low-poly geometry rendered into a small buffer and scaled back up, grey concrete with yellow floor markings, and a black hole in the sky whose shader is lifted straight out of Gargantua.
Nothing saves. A session runs two to four hours and starts from nothing the next time, which is the point, the fun is in rebuilding the line better, not in inheriting it.

projects.name: G-Doodle
projects.blurb: A transformer that draws. Type what you want in Polish and it sketches it stroke by stroke.
body: The third model in the family, after G-Micro and G-Images, trained from scratch over 345 categories of drawing. It does not produce an image in one shot, it emits strokes in order, so you watch the picture being drawn rather than appear.
It is also the first of the family that needs nothing running at home. G-Micro and G-Images both go quiet when the Mac sleeps; this one is small enough to run in the browser it is displayed in.

projects.name: Hollowtree
projects.blurb: One to three players, each of them a queen bee, sharing one hive inside a hollow tree.
body: You fly as a queen over a meadow, gather pollen, and return to a hive that everyone shares. Workers follow you in a swarm rather than being assigned to flowers, so a bigger swarm simply covers more blossoms at once, and the comb you build is a hex grid of cells with different jobs that reward good neighbours.

The strategy lives in the calendar. Ten-plus plant species open and close on their own schedules, a season lasts two real days and a year lasts eight, so the map you learned last week is not the map you are flying now.
There is no combat. Hornets are a real threat, but the answer is structural, narrow the entrance, set traps, post guards. A queen runs; she does not fight.

projects.name: Narew Labs
projects.blurb: Chat with a language model trained from scratch, running on a MacBook, reached from anywhere.
body: G-Micro is a 110-million-parameter language model built from nothing: the tokenizer, the training loop and the Polish corpus are all ours. This is the app you talk to it through.

The page itself computes nothing. It writes a task into a database, a MacBook picks it up, runs the model and streams the answer back token by token. Both sides dial out, so no port is ever opened on the Mac, deliberately chosen over a tunnel.
The same window also edits photos with G-Images, a second model of ours. Ask for black and white or a blur and it makes the change directly, with no service in the middle.

projects.name: SKI Together
projects.blurb: A day at a ski resort for two to five people, on snow that remembers every turn you carved.
body: The mountain has three runs, a five-seat chairlift, a drag lift, a rental shop and a cafe, and up to five people ski it together. Difficulty comes from the line rather than the label: the blue traverses across the slope, the black falls straight down it.

The snow is the real system. A grid of five million cells, one every half metre, remembers both its condition and how deep the ruts are, and the same two arrays feed the physics on the processor and the shader on the graphics card, so the groove you can see is the groove you can feel. After forty runs a popular line drops to fifteen percent condition with ruts nearly thirty centimetres deep, while the snow two metres to the side is untouched. Nothing heals on its own; a groomer has to go out and fix it.

The skiing physics run on that height field rather than on a rigid body. Straight-lining measures 61 km/h, tucking on race skis 82, full carving 48, powder 11, and what actually decides a jump is the angle you hit the ramp at, not how tall the ramp is.

projects.name: Smendiłendi
projects.blurb: A printed robot dog on four servos and an ESP32, the first project here whose output is a physical object.
body: A small, light quadruped printed on a Bambu Lab X1C in ordinary PLA, driven by four hobby servos and a microcontroller. The scope is poses, touch and simple movement rather than dynamic walking.

It is the first project here where the feedback loop needs a person. The model can be changed from a keyboard, but measuring whether the printed part actually fits requires somebody standing at the printer with calipers, and that changes how the work is planned.

projects.name: Gzowo Builders
projects.blurb: Build a vehicle out of blocks, wheels and pistons, then drive it until something snaps off.
body: A creative sandbox with real physics: you place parts on a quarter-metre grid, wire pistons and hinges to buttons and timers, and drive whatever you came up with. There is no survival mode and there never will be, the whole game is the workshop.

The interesting part is what holds a build together. Every construction is one rigid body, and the joints between parts are a graph; when a bridge in that graph carries more force than it can hold, that piece tears off on its own. Nothing is scripted, an overloaded cantilever fails because it is overloaded.

Wheels are raycast rather than physical bodies, which is why a car at 40 km/h through a slalom keeps all four corners instead of shaking itself apart. It runs co-op over the local network, with one machine acting as the authority on physics and running exactly the same code the browser runs.

projects.name: G-Mini
projects.blurb: The second rung of the ladder: 178 million parameters, warm-started from G-Micro, trained in one week of free GPU time.
body: The successor to G-Micro, aimed squarely at the things G-Micro gets wrong, with a hard budget: a single week of free Kaggle quota on two T4s. Every choice in the configuration came from a measurement rather than a guess.

Warm-starting from the smaller model rather than beginning at random is what makes the budget work, the new network inherits what the old one already learned about Polish and spends its week on what it does not know.

projects.name: Gzowo TV
projects.blurb: An Apple TV for the family plot, every streaming service in one launcher, on a Mac plugged into the television.
body: A video aggregator built for the house in Gzowo: one grid, one remote, and the services behind it opening full-screen in a kiosk browser instead of demanding a different device each.

Two macOS traps cost real time here and are worth writing down. Renaming the application bundle poisoned its entry in the system launcher, opening it reported success and started nothing, with an empty log and no error anywhere; only a fresh bundle identifier fixed it. And because macOS refuses to let a bundled app overwrite a file another process created under the downloads folder, the server died instantly on every start until its log moved elsewhere.

projects.name: Airwave
projects.blurb: An instrument you play with your hands in the air, in front of a webcam. No hardware.
body: Your right hand sets the pitch and snaps to a pentatonic scale so it is hard to sound bad; your left hand is the volume. Fingers pick the octave, a fist morphs the timbre, a pinch adds vibrato, and your mouth works as a wah pedal.
Hand tracking runs locally in the browser and the sound is synthesised in the page, so nothing about you leaves the machine. Desktop only, it needs a camera and a real amount of light.

projects.name: Voxel Demolition
projects.blurb: A destruction sandbox with twenty-five tools and co-op for four. Runs on a server at home.
body: Everything in the plaza is made of voxels and everything comes apart: hammers, charges, a shotgun and a launcher, plus builder tools that put material back. Twenty-five of them, grouped so you can cycle by category rather than hunting through a list.

Up to four people share one world through a headless Node server that holds the authoritative state. That is also why there is no link to play here yet, the server runs on a laptop at home, so for now the code is what you can look at.

projects.name: G-Images
projects.blurb: A diffusion model for editing photos, trained from scratch, small enough to run on a laptop.
body: The second model in the family. You point a camera at something, say what you want changed, and it changes the frame locally, no service in the middle, no upload. It answers to the voice assistant, which is where the request usually comes from.

Like the rest of the family it is trained from nothing rather than adapted from an existing model, which puts a hard ceiling on how good it can be at this size and makes the interesting question how much can be had from seventy million parameters.

projects.name: G-Micro
projects.blurb: A 117-million-parameter language model in Polish, trained from scratch, tokenizer, corpus and training loop included.
body: The first model in the family and the first rung of a ladder that runs G-Micro, G-Mini, G-Core, G-Mega. Nothing here is a fine-tune of somebody else's weights: the tokenizer, the Polish corpus and the training loop were all built for it, which was the whole point, the aim was to have a model that works and to understand every layer of why it does.
It runs offline on a MacBook. Training happens on free cloud GPUs, because the hardware here has neither the memory nor the tensor cores to do it in any reasonable time.

projects.name: MJJ Archives
projects.blurb: Watch Billie Jean at Motown 25 rebuilt in 3D, together, with the television cuts replayed shot for shot.
body: Up to four people join a room and spawn as avatars in a theatre. The host starts the show, a 3D Michael Jackson dances the full four minutes and fifty-seven seconds locked to the real audio, and everyone's camera snaps to a director cam that reproduces the 1983 broadcast's thirty-seven cuts in order.

The motion is captured from the broadcast footage itself rather than animated by hand. That was not the first plan: a fully hand-authored choreography was built, locked to the beat, and thrown away for being ten times worse, the roughness of real capture carries the character. What shipped is the capture with three surgical repairs: the root is anchored only where tracking is confident, gaps are filled from a motion graph of the same performance, and the moonwalk glides on an authored path while the legs stay captured.

Because video and audio from the source run to the same length, the two stay in step across the whole song, and the animation follows the audio playhead rather than the frame clock, so a slow machine drops frames instead of drifting out of time.

projects.name: Untitled Civ Game
projects.blurb: One to three gods share a single city and take down a rival built by the machine.
body: A cooperative real-time strategy game where the players are not opponents. Everyone runs the same city, the enemy is a bot settlement growing on the other side of the map, and a match lands somewhere between twenty and forty minutes with pause available at any point.
Built in a single pass and complete, but it needs its own server process to run, so there is no public link yet, the source is here and it starts with one command.

projects.name: Gargantua
projects.blurb: Co-op zero-gravity spacewalk next to a black hole. Push off carefully; there is no brake.
body: You move by pushing off surfaces and firing short bursts, which means every mistake keeps travelling. Working together is less about coordination than about not sending your partner spinning.
The black hole is the reason for the whole thing: light bends around it, and the closer you drift the more the view stops behaving the way your eyes expect.

projects.name: Cruise Control
projects.blurb: A precision driving game with retro pixel post-processing, moving hazards and a shop.
body: Steer through courses where the obstacles move with you rather than sitting still. Version 2 added seven levels, a sensitivity setting, an economy with a shop, and three-player multiplayer.
The look comes from a post-processing pass that resolves the whole frame down to chunky pixels, so the clean vector shapes underneath arrive looking like something from a much older machine.

projects.name: Untitled Pogo Game
projects.blurb: Fifteen levels of pogo-stick parkour, playable together, installable as an app.
body: One button, one stick, fifteen levels that get mean quickly. The jump is a spring rather than a fixed arc, so timing the compression matters more than timing the press.
It runs as an installable web app and has a co-op mode, which turns the harder levels into a race where both of you are usually wrong.

projects.name: Backrooms
projects.blurb: Yellow rooms, buzzing lights, and a maze that does not care whether you get out.
body: A first-person walk through an endless office that never quite repeats. There is no map and no marker; the only thing you build up is a sense of which corridor you have already ruined an hour on.
The tension is carried almost entirely by sound and by light that hums at the wrong frequency, there is very little in the way of enemies, and it does not need them.

projects.name: Gzowo AI
projects.blurb: A voice assistant for the house in Gzowo, speak to it in Polish and it answers in real time.
body: A Jarvis-style assistant with a black and white interface and a sphere for a face that shifts between idle, talking and showing. It listens and replies in Polish through a realtime audio model, remembers across sessions, and reaches into the house and the other projects here rather than being a chat window.
It runs on a Mac at home and costs nothing to operate. When the Mac sleeps the assistant degrades gently instead of breaking, the parts that need the machine go quiet and the rest keeps answering.

projects.name: GSP Brand Kit
projects.blurb: The visual identity behind GSP, logo, colours and type, in one page you can download from.
body: The brand kit for Gzowo Space Program: the mark, the palette, the typefaces and the rules for putting them together, published as a single page with the files attached.
The look is deliberately severe, black ground, condensed capitals for headlines, a monospace for data, and nothing decorative. It is the identity the rocket site runs on.

projects.name: Gzowo Bowling
projects.blurb: Bowling on a laptop, thrown with a phone. Scan the code and your phone becomes the ball.
body: The laptop shows the lane; your phone is the controller. You scan a code, and the swing of your arm is the throw, the motion sensors in the phone are the input, so nobody has to learn a control scheme.
Under the alley is a proper physics simulation with three.js and Rapier, built without a bundler: modules straight from a CDN, which is the pattern most of the games here still use.

projects.name: Modular
projects.blurb: Drop sixteen kinds of building on a plot and watch a town assemble itself around them.
body: A calm builder: you place buildings, they connect, and the place slowly turns into somewhere. Saves persist and you can build alongside someone else.

Most of the work went into the parts you do not notice, shadows that make the models sit on the ground properly, an audio bus so the ambience does not stack into noise, and a pixel ratio that drops itself on weaker machines instead of stuttering.

projects.name: Galeria Gzowo
projects.blurb: A gallery for the place the rest of this site is named after.
body: Photographs from Gzowo, put somewhere they can actually be looked at rather than buried in a phone.
Small, quick and deliberately plain, the pictures are the whole point.

projects.name: Narew
projects.blurb: One real property by the Narew: paddle it, dig it, ride a jet ski through it, or watch TV indoors.
body: One HTML file holding a three.js world: a single property in Gzowo on the Narew, the house on it, a carport, the meadow and the river below. The terrain is not invented. Elevations come from a Copernicus digital elevation model, and the river channel, the oxbow lake and the drainage ditches are polylines traced from OpenStreetMap and carved into the heightfield, so the shape of the water matches the real place. The ground is also editable: an excavator and a shovel cut real holes into a one-metre mesh, with flat bottoms you can climb down into, and the coarse grid underneath is pushed out of the way so the two never fight.

The water carries traffic. Three kayaks lie on the bank and a jet ski is moored in the channel; the jet ski leaves expanding rings behind it, and those rings are not decoration, they are read back by the kayaks, which lift and pitch when a wake reaches them. Kayak hulls refuse to leave water deeper than thirty centimetres, so the river keeps you in it.

The television in the glass house is a canvas texture redrawn in place: live weather for Gzowo from open-meteo, short films drawn frame by frame, a shelf of YouTube links behind a password, and NAREBLOX, eleven small games. Nine are drawn on that canvas; two are separate three.js scenes rendered to a texture, so the set displays real 3D from inside a 3D world. Every one of the eleven is multiplayer. Facing the set there is now a sofa with a man in swimming trunks sitting on it, dripping, phone in hand, sit down and the view cuts to his screen, which plays a vertical feed of one person's videos and nothing else.

The place is populated. A neighbour walks a fixed round of the property and stops to talk when you stand near him; a sounder of ten wild boar roots through the meadow and bolts as a group when you get within eleven metres; five raccoons dance in a ring around the campfire and speed up when it is lit. A keypad by the door takes a two-digit code, and the right one brings a man on horseback across the meadow with a cigarette in his mouth. Their clothes are photographs of linen, cloth and leather from CC0 libraries, cut to 512 pixels, with code-drawn weave as the fallback if the folder is missing.

Around that: characters are GLTF models with blended idle, walk and run clips, multiplayer runs peer to peer over PeerJS with the host relaying positions, and wind is patched into existing materials by swapping their shader, so grass and tree crowns bend from the base with a phase taken from world position. The interface is in Polish, the way it was written.

projects.name: Spider-Man: New York
body: A third-person Spider-Man game written as plain JavaScript modules on top of three.js. The city is a procedurally built Manhattan at sunset, day or night: nine districts, Central Park with a pond, rivers, street traffic with signals and pedestrians, all drawn from generated textures with no image files.

Movement is the point. Swinging uses a real pendulum around a web anchor that is picked by raycasting the buildings, so you can hold one button and chain swings; you can also run up walls, zip forward in mid-air, and fling yourself to rooftop ledges with a point-launch. Combat has a four-hit combo, launchers and air combos, web-wrapping, dodges that slow time, a focus meter for finishers, and thugs that shoot, swing bats or block until you web them.

Every character is one smooth skinned mesh on a skeleton with five-fingered hands that change between open, fist and web-shooter poses, and the suits are painted at load time with embossed webbing. The game also has a Rhino boss fight, ring races, car chases you ride on the roof of, a skill tree, 15 unlockable suits, a map, cutscenes and generated music, and it runs from a single bundled file with no server.

rockets.title: Rockets
rockets.lead: Gzowo Space Program (GSP) is where the things that fly live. Model rockets built by hand and launched from a family field in Gzowo, Poland, with onboard cameras, parachutes and a lot of waiting for the wind to calm down.

fleet.name: Gzofajfus Mini Mk I
fleet.blurb: The first rocket of the Mini series: a miniature experimental platform with very little mass.
photos: On the launch rail, seen from below

fleet.name: Gzofajfus Classic Mk II
fleet.blurb: The first rocket of the full-size Classic series and a proven platform for tests. Its parachute deployed on the first flight.

fleet.name: Gzofajfus Classic Mk III
fleet.blurb: The newest Classic. The nose cone has a bay for an AirTag, so the rocket can be found after it lands.

fleet.name: The Orange Beauty
fleet.blurb: The only rocket of its kind in the fleet, and the one with the best launch footage.

fleet.name: TBH Mk I
fleet.blurb: The first of the all-black rockets. Its one mission is to come down safely on a parachute.
